notes.front: What is Envoy, in an Istio mesh?
notes.back: A high-performance proxy, written in C++, that mediates all inbound and outbound traffic for every service in the mesh.
notes.explanation: Istio uses an extended version of Envoy, and Envoy proxies are the only Istio components that touch data plane traffic.
notes.example: Like a reverse proxy placed in front of one web app, but here one copy sits beside every service and handles its traffic both ways.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Envoy”
notes.evidence: Istio uses an extended version of the Envoy proxy. Envoy is a high-performance proxy developed in C++ to mediate all inbound and outbound traffic for all services in the service mesh. Envoy proxies are the only Istio components that interact with data plane traffic.

notes.front: What is istiod?
notes.back: Istio’s control plane component. It provides service discovery, configuration and certificate management for the proxies.
notes.explanation: istiod turns high-level routing rules into Envoy-specific configuration and sends it to the proxies while they run.
notes.example: Like an air traffic control tower: it never carries passengers itself, but tells every aircraft (proxy) where to go.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Istiod”
notes.evidence: Istiod provides service discovery, configuration and certificate management. Istiod converts high level routing rules that control traffic behavior into Envoy-specific configurations, and propagates them to the sidecars at runtime.

notes.front: What is Istio’s sidecar mode?
notes.back: A data plane mode that deploys an Envoy proxy alongside each pod you start in the cluster (or beside services on VMs).
notes.explanation: It is one of Istio’s two main data plane modes, and you can opt certain namespaces or workloads into each mode.
notes.example: Like giving every office its own receptionist, rather than one front desk per building.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, introduction
notes.evidence: sidecar mode, which deploys an Envoy proxy along with each pod that you start in your cluster, or running alongside services running on VMs.

notes.front: What is Istio’s ambient mode?
notes.back: A data plane mode that uses a per-node Layer 4 proxy and, optionally, a per-namespace Layer 7 proxy.
notes.explanation: The layers let you adopt Istio step by step: from no mesh, to a secure Layer 4 overlay, to full Layer 7 processing, namespace by namespace.
notes.example: Like a building with one shared security desk per floor, plus an optional concierge only for the tenants who ask for one.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, introduction
notes.evidence: In ambient mode, Istio implements its features using a per-node Layer 4 (L4) proxy, and optionally a per-namespace Layer 7 (L7) proxy. This layered approach allows you to adopt Istio in a more incremental fashion, smoothly transitioning from no mesh, to a secure L4 overlay, to full L7 processing and policy

notes.front: What is ztunnel?
notes.back: The Zero Trust tunnel: a purpose-built, per-node proxy that powers Istio’s ambient data plane mode.
notes.explanation: ztunnel securely connects and authenticates the workloads within the mesh.
notes.example: Like one shared, armoured courier van per street that carries every household’s parcels, instead of each house running its own van.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “ztunnel”
notes.evidence: The ztunnel (Zero Trust tunnel) component is a purpose-built, per-node proxy that powers Istio’s ambient data plane mode. Ztunnel is responsible for securely connecting and authenticating workloads within the mesh.

notes.front: What is xDS, in Istio?
notes.back: The set of APIs through which proxies, such as ztunnel, get configuration and discovery information from istiod.
notes.explanation: The ztunnel troubleshooting guide names xDS as the channel between istiod and ztunnel, and lets you view istiod’s xDS resources for each ztunnel.
notes.example: Like a subscription feed: the proxy stays connected and istiod sends it the configuration it should be running.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Troubleshoot issues with ztunnel”, introduction
notes.evidence: The ztunnel proxy gets configuration and discovery information from the istiod control plane via xDS APIs.

notes.front: What is HBONE?
notes.back: The HTTP CONNECT-based traffic tunnelling protocol that carries ambient mode’s secure overlay at the transport layer.
notes.explanation: The “secure overlay” is the set of Layer 4 functions that ztunnel provides; HBONE is how it moves that traffic.
notes.example: Like sending each letter inside a sealed, addressed courier pouch rather than as a loose postcard.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “ztunnel”
notes.evidence: The term “secure overlay” is used to collectively describe the set of L4 networking functions implemented in an ambient mesh via the ztunnel proxy. At the transport layer, this is implemented via an HTTP CONNECT-based traffic tunneling protocol called HBONE.

notes.front: What is a waypoint proxy?
notes.back: An optional Envoy-based proxy deployment that adds Layer 7 processing to a defined set of workloads in ambient mode.
notes.explanation: Waypoints are installed, upgraded and scaled separately from the applications; an application owner should be unaware of them.
notes.example: Like a customs checkpoint you only build on the routes that need parcels opened and inspected.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, introduction
notes.evidence: A waypoint proxy is an optional deployment of the Envoy-based proxy to add Layer 7 (L7) processing to a defined set of workloads. Waypoint proxies are installed, upgraded and scaled independently from applications; an application owner should be unaware of their existence.

notes.front: In Istio, the {{c1::control plane}} manages and configures the proxies to route traffic.
notes.back: The control plane.
notes.explanation: The mesh is split into two planes; the data plane’s proxies carry the traffic, while the control plane configures them.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, introduction
notes.evidence: An Istio service mesh is logically split into a data plane and a control plane.

notes.front: In sidecar mode, which component makes up the control plane, and what makes up the data plane?
notes.back: Control plane: istiod. Data plane: the Envoy proxies deployed as sidecars beside each service.
notes.explanation: The sidecar proxies mediate all traffic between microservices and report telemetry; istiod configures them.

image.alt: Diagram of Istio in sidecar mode. A control plane box at the top holds istiod, labelled discovery, configuration and certificates. Below, a data plane box holds two pods; each pod contains a service and an Envoy proxy sidecar. Dashed arrows run from istiod to each Envoy proxy, labelled configuration pushed to the proxies, and a solid arrow labelled mesh traffic runs from one pod’s Envoy proxy to the other’s.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Istio documentation, “Architecture” (Istio architecture in sidecar mode)

notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, introduction and “Components”
notes.evidence: The data plane is composed of a set of intelligent proxies (Envoy) deployed as sidecars. These proxies mediate and control all network communication between microservices. They also collect and report telemetry on all mesh traffic.

notes.front: A team wants mesh features for a legacy service but cannot change its code. According to Istio’s architecture page, what does the sidecar proxy model allow?
notes.back: A: adding Istio capabilities to the existing deployment without rearchitecting or rewriting code.
notes.choices:
A) Istio capabilities can be added without rearchitecting or rewriting code
B) Only services rewritten to call the Envoy API can join
C) The service must be rebuilt with an Istio library linked in
notes.choicesExplained: B and C both require code changes, which the sidecar model is described as avoiding: the proxy sits beside the service instead.
notes.explanation: The Envoy sidecar augments the service from the outside, so the service’s own code is left as it is.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Envoy”
notes.evidence: The sidecar proxy model also allows you to add Istio capabilities to an existing deployment without requiring you to rearchitect or rewrite code.

notes.front: Which istiod role turns high-level routing rules into Envoy-specific configuration and sends it to the sidecars at runtime?
notes.back: Configuration.
notes.explanation: The Traffic Management API instructs istiod to refine this Envoy configuration for finer control of traffic.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Istiod”
notes.evidence: Istiod converts high level routing rules that control traffic behavior into Envoy-specific configurations, and propagates them to the sidecars at runtime.

notes.front: Which istiod role abstracts platform-specific mechanisms, such as those of Kubernetes or VMs, into a standard format any Envoy-API sidecar can consume?
notes.back: Service discovery.
notes.explanation: Because the format is standard, Istio can support discovery for several environments, such as Kubernetes or VMs.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Istiod”
notes.evidence: It abstracts platform-specific service discovery mechanisms and synthesizes them into a standard format that any sidecar conforming with the Envoy API can consume. Istio can support discovery for multiple environments such as Kubernetes or VMs.

notes.front: Which istiod role lets it act as a certificate authority?
notes.back: Certificate management: istiod generates the certificates that allow secure mTLS in the data plane.
notes.explanation: This sits alongside istiod’s other two roles, service discovery and configuration.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Istiod”
notes.evidence: Istiod acts as a Certificate Authority (CA) and generates certificates to allow secure mTLS communication in the data plane.

notes.front: An operator changes a routing rule and wants to know which part of Istio will translate it for the proxies. Which is it?
notes.back: B: istiod, which converts routing rules into Envoy configuration and pushes it to the proxies.
notes.choices:
A) The Envoy sidecar of the calling pod
B) istiod
C) The Kubernetes Service object
notes.choicesExplained: B receives the finished configuration rather than producing it. C is a Kubernetes object, not an Istio component, and does not configure proxies.
notes.explanation: Translating high-level rules into Envoy-specific configuration is istiod’s configuration role.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, section “Istiod”
notes.evidence: Istiod converts high level routing rules that control traffic behavior into Envoy-specific configurations, and propagates them to the sidecars at runtime.

notes.front: What trade-off does Istio’s documentation name for sidecar mode?
notes.back: It is well understood and thoroughly battle-tested, but comes with a resource cost and operational overhead.
notes.explanation: Istio has been built on the sidecar pattern since its first release in 2017.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Sidecar mode”
notes.evidence: Istio has been built on the sidecar pattern from its first release in 2017. Sidecar mode is well understood and thoroughly battle-tested, but comes with a resource cost and operational overhead.

notes.front: As of Istio {{c1::1.22}}, ambient mode is production-ready for single cluster use cases.
notes.explanation: Ambient mode was launched in 2022 to address shortcomings that users reported with sidecar mode.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Ambient mode”
notes.evidence: Launched in 2022, ambient mode was built to address the shortcomings reported by users of sidecar mode. As of Istio 1.22, it is production-ready for single cluster use cases.

notes.front: Can pods using sidecar mode and pods using ambient mode be in the same mesh?
notes.back: Yes. An “ambient mesh” is installed with support for ambient mode and can hold pods using either data plane.
notes.explanation: The two data plane modes interoperate, so users can mix capabilities as their needs change.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “How it works”
notes.evidence: Pods and workloads using sidecar mode can co-exist within the same mesh as pods that use ambient mode. The term “ambient mesh” refers to an Istio mesh that was installed with support for ambient mode, and so can support mesh pods that use either type of data plane.

notes.front: How does adding workloads to the mesh differ between sidecar mode and ambient mode?
notes.back: Sidecar: label the namespace and restart all pods to add sidecars. Ambient: label the namespace; no pod restart is needed.
notes.explanation: In ambient mode the namespace label is enough, and existing pods keep running.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Choosing between sidecar and ambient”
notes.evidence: Adding workloads to the meshLabel a namespace and restart all pods to have sidecars addedLabel a namespace - no pod restart required

notes.front: How many Layer 7 processing steps does a request take in sidecar mode, and in ambient mode with a waypoint?
notes.back: Sidecar: two (source and destination sidecar). Ambient: one (the destination waypoint).
notes.explanation: In ambient mode, policies are enforced by the destination waypoint rather than by proxies at both ends.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Choosing between sidecar and ambient”
notes.evidence: L7 processing steps2 (source and destination sidecar)1 (destination waypoint)

notes.front: An attacker compromises an application pod. In which data plane mode does that give them access to mesh keys?
notes.back: B: sidecar mode. In ambient mode, a compromised application pod does not give access to mesh keys.
notes.choices:
A) Ambient mode only
B) Sidecar mode only
C) Both modes
notes.choicesExplained: B has it the wrong way round: ambient keys are held by the node agent, not by the pod. C is wrong because the comparison table answers “No” for ambient.
notes.explanation: In sidecar mode each workload holds its own keys; in ambient mode each node agent holds only the keys for workloads on its node.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Choosing between sidecar and ambient”
notes.evidence: Security modelStrongest: each workload has its own keysStrong: each node agent has only the keys for workloads on that node Compromised application pod gives access to mesh keysYesNo

notes.front: In ambient mode, how is extensibility provided, and which API is not supported?
notes.back: Via WebAssembly plugins, which require a waypoint. The EnvoyFilter API is not supported.
notes.explanation: Sidecar mode has the full Istio feature set for extensibility; ambient mode narrows it to plugins running on waypoints.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Choosing between sidecar and ambient”
notes.evidence: ExtensibilityFull Istio feature setVia WebAssembly plugins (requires using waypoint) The EnvoyFilter API is not supported.

notes.front: Why does Istio suggest meeting a service’s requirements at Layer 4 where you can?
notes.back: Processing protocols at Layer 7 costs substantially more than processing packets at Layer 4, so a mesh at Layer 4 is much cheaper.
notes.explanation: The cost gap is the basis of the advice: requirements that Layer 4 can meet are delivered more cheaply there.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Layer 4 vs Layer 7 features”
notes.evidence: The overhead for processing protocols at Layer 7 is substantially higher than processing network packets at Layer 4. For a given service, if your requirements can be met at L4, service mesh can be delivered at substantially lower cost.

notes.front: A rule says service A may call /orders on service B only when the caller carries valid end-user credentials. Which layer must enforce it?
notes.back: B: Layer 7. At Layer 4, per-user settings cannot be applied.
notes.choices:
A) Layer 4
B) Layer 7
C) Either layer
notes.choicesExplained: A and C fail because Layer 4 authorization is network- and identity-based only, and end-user authentication is not available at Layer 4.
notes.explanation: Rules about request methods, paths and end-user credentials are the “full policy” that Istio places at Layer 7.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Security”
notes.evidence: Full policy, e.g.: A can GET /foo on B only with valid end-user credentials containing the READ scope. End-user authenticationN/A—we can't apply per-user settings.

notes.front: Can workloads on virtual machines use ambient mode?
notes.back: Not yet: VM support is listed as available in sidecar mode but not yet implemented in ambient mode.
notes.explanation: The same list names multi-cluster installations and multi-network support, among others, as sidecar-only for now.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, section “Unsupported features”
notes.evidence: The following features are available in sidecar mode, but not yet implemented in ambient mode: Sidecar-to-waypoint interoperability Multi-cluster installations Multi-network support VM support

notes.front: Does ztunnel terminate workload HTTP traffic or parse HTTP headers?
notes.back: No. ztunnel is scoped to Layer 3 and 4 functions such as mTLS, authentication, Layer 4 authorization and telemetry.
notes.explanation: ztunnel is written in Rust and intentionally kept to Layers 3 and 4.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “ztunnel”; “Configure waypoint proxies”
notes.evidence: The ztunnel proxy is written in Rust and is intentionally scoped to handle L3 and L4 functions such as mTLS, authentication, L4 authorization and telemetry. Ztunnel does not terminate workload HTTP traffic or parse workload HTTP headers.

notes.front: In ambient mode, Istio’s data plane uses node-level ztunnel proxies deployed as a {{c1::DaemonSet}}.
notes.back: DaemonSet.
notes.explanation: Each node therefore runs its own ztunnel, which mediates all traffic that the mesh services send and receive.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Sidecar or ambient?”, data plane definition
notes.evidence: node-level ztunnel proxies deployed as a DaemonSet to mediate and control all traffic that your mesh services send and receive.

notes.front: Two ambient-mode pods run on the same node, and one calls the other. Does the traffic pass through ztunnel?
notes.back: C: yes; local traffic also traverses the node’s ztunnel, so Layer 4 authorization and telemetry apply just as across nodes.
notes.choices:
A) No, same-node traffic bypasses ztunnel
B) Only if a waypoint proxy is deployed
C) Yes, it traverses the local ztunnel
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the page states that local traffic traverses the local ztunnel. C is wrong: no waypoint is needed for Layer 4 handling by ztunnel.
notes.explanation: Sending local traffic through ztunnel means Layer 4 functions are enforced identically whether or not traffic crosses a node boundary.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, section “Dataplane example for Layer 4 traffic”
notes.evidence: also traverses the local ztunnel proxy instance, so that L4 traffic management functions such as L4 Authorization and L4 Telemetry will be enforced identically on traffic, whether or not it crosses a node boundary.

notes.front: Which identities does ztunnel use for mTLS between workloads, and which certificate requests does the certificate authority reject?
notes.back: A separate certificate per workload identity on its node, never its own. The certificate authority rejects requests for identities not on that node.
notes.explanation: ztunnel authenticates to the certificate authority with its own identity, but asks for the identity of each workload it proxies.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, section “Dataplane details: Identity”
notes.evidence: Ztunnel’s own identity is never used for mTLS connections between workloads. When fetching certificates, ztunnel will authenticate to the CA with its own identity, but request the identity of another workload. Critically, the CA must enforce that the ztunnel has permission to request that identity. Requests for identities not running on the node are rejected.

notes.front: In ambient mode, where are HBONE tunnels actually encapsulated and decapsulated?
notes.back: In the network namespace of the source pod and of the destination pod, not between the two ztunnel proxies.
notes.explanation: ztunnel still handles HBONE, but it does so from inside the pods’ network namespaces.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, section “Dataplane example for Layer 4 traffic”
notes.evidence: the tunnels are in fact between the source and destination pods. Traffic is HBONE encapsulated and encrypted in the network namespace of the source pod itself, and eventually decapsulated and decrypted in the network namespace of the destination pod on the destination worker node.

notes.front: What kind of traffic do Istio waypoints receive?
notes.back: Only HBONE traffic.
notes.explanation: Having accepted it, the waypoint checks the traffic is for a Pod or Service that uses it, then enforces Layer 7 policies.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, sections “Dataplane details” and “In Mesh routing with Waypoint enabled”
notes.evidence: Istio waypoints exclusively receive HBONE traffic. Upon receiving a request, the waypoint will ensure that the traffic is for a Pod or Service which uses it. Having accepted the traffic, the waypoint will then enforce L7 policies

notes.front: Two ambient-mode pods on different nodes exchange traffic, with no waypoint involved. How does ztunnel carry it?
notes.back: A: in an HBONE tunnel, the HTTP CONNECT-based protocol of the secure overlay.
notes.choices:
A) In an HBONE tunnel
B) As plain traffic with no tunnel
C) Through a sidecar in each pod
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: traffic between mesh workloads is tunnelled and encrypted. C is wrong: ambient pods have no sidecars; ztunnel does the tunnelling.
notes.explanation: HBONE is how ztunnel’s secure overlay moves Layer 4 traffic at the transport layer.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “ztunnel”
notes.evidence: At the transport layer, this is implemented via an HTTP CONNECT-based traffic tunneling protocol called HBONE.

notes.front: An ambient pod calls a Service that is in the mesh and uses a waypoint. What does the node-local ztunnel do with the request?
notes.back: The node-local ztunnel upgrades it to an encrypted HBONE tunnel and forwards it to that waypoint for Layer 7 policy.
notes.explanation: The request is first transparently redirected to the node-local ztunnel, which decides where and how to forward it.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, section “Outbound”
notes.evidence: If the destination has a waypoint proxy, in addition to being upgraded to HBONE, the request will be forwarded to that waypoint for L7 policy enforcement.

notes.front: A pod outside the mesh calls a waypoint-enabled destination. Does the request pass through the waypoint?
notes.back: B: no. It goes directly to the destination, because an out-of-mesh workload knows nothing about waypoints.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, ztunnel always inserts the waypoint
B) No, it goes directly to the destination
C) Yes, but only for Service traffic
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong: only a source in the ambient mesh has its ztunnel send the request through the waypoint.
notes.explanation: The waypoint is enforced by the source’s ztunnel, so a source with no ztunnel skips it.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, section “Inbound”
notes.evidence: When the destination is waypoint enabled, if the source is in ambient mesh, the source’s ztunnel ensures the request will go through the waypoint where policy is enforced. However, a workload outside of the mesh doesn’t know anything about waypoint proxies therefore it sends requests directly to the destination without going through any waypoint proxy

notes.front: A pod is added to the ambient data plane by setting the label {{c1::istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient}}.
notes.back: istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
notes.explanation: With this label the pod is “In Mesh”: ztunnel intercepts its traffic at Layer 4 and Layer 4 policies can be enforced.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, workload categories
notes.evidence: In this mode, L4 policies can be enforced for pod traffic. This mode can be enabled by setting the istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient label.

notes.front: You want a namespace’s pods in the ambient mesh with Layer 4 security only. Which label do you set?
notes.back: B: istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient.
notes.choices:
A) istio.io/use-waypoint=<name>
B) istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
C) istio-injection=enabled
notes.choicesExplained: B attaches a waypoint for Layer 7 policy, which is not asked for. C turns on sidecar injection, the other data plane mode.
notes.explanation: Labelling with dataplane-mode=ambient puts pods “In Mesh”, where Layer 4 policies apply without any waypoint.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient data plane”, workload categories
notes.evidence: In this mode, L4 policies can be enforced for pod traffic. This mode can be enabled by setting the istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient label.

notes.front: What are two Layer 7 mesh functions that require a waypoint proxy in ambient mode?
notes.back: Any two, for example: HTTP routing and load balancing; authorization based on HTTP headers; HTTP metrics or access logging.
notes.explanation: The documentation groups these functions under traffic management, security and observability.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Do you need a waypoint proxy?”
notes.evidence: If your applications require any of the following L7 mesh functions, you will need to use a waypoint proxy: Traffic management: HTTP routing & load balancing, circuit breaking, rate limiting, fault injection, retries, timeouts Security: Rich authorization policies based on L7 primitives such as request type or HTTP header Observability: HTTP metrics, access logging, tracing

notes.front: An ambient-mode team needs mTLS between services, Layer 4 authorization and Layer 4 telemetry, and nothing more. What do they deploy?
notes.back: B: ztunnel only, which is the default; no waypoint proxy is required.
notes.choices:
A) ztunnel and a waypoint proxy
B) ztunnel only
C) A sidecar in each pod
notes.choicesExplained: B adds Layer 7 processing the team does not need. C switches to sidecar mode, which the team does not need for these Layer 4 features.
notes.explanation: Zero-trust networking, Layer 4 authorization and Layer 4 telemetry are all handled by the ztunnel secure overlay.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, section “Waypoint proxies”
notes.evidence: Zero Trust networking via mutual-TLS, encrypted and tunneled data transport of client application traffic, L4 authorization, L4 telemetryztunnel only (default)

notes.front: What Kubernetes resource deploys a waypoint proxy, and which gatewayClassName does it use?
notes.back: A Kubernetes Gateway API Gateway resource with gatewayClassName istio-waypoint.
notes.explanation: Once the resource is applied, istiod deploys and manages the waypoint’s deployment and service automatically.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Deploy a waypoint proxy”
notes.evidence: Note the Gateway resource has a gatewayClassName of istio-waypoint, which instantiates an Istio-managed waypoint.

notes.front: Which istioctl command deploys a waypoint named “waypoint” into the default namespace and enrols the namespace at the same time?
notes.back: istioctl waypoint apply -n default --enroll-namespace
notes.explanation: The --enroll-namespace flag adds the istio.io/use-waypoint label to the namespace for you.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Use a waypoint proxy”
notes.evidence: If you use istioctl to deploy your namespace waypoint, you can use the --enroll-namespace parameter to automatically label a namespace

notes.front: By default, which traffic does a waypoint handle, and which label on the Gateway sets this?
notes.back: Only traffic addressed to services in its namespace; the istio.io/waypoint-for label (default value: service).
notes.explanation: Traffic aimed at a pod alone is rare and often internal, such as Prometheus scraping, where extra Layer 7 overhead may not be wanted.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Waypoint traffic types”
notes.evidence: By default, a waypoint will only handle traffic destined for services in its namespaces. This choice was made because traffic directed at a pod alone is rare, and often used for internal purposes such as Prometheus scraping, and the extra overhead of L7 processing may not be desired.

notes.front: Which istio.io/waypoint-for value makes a waypoint handle traffic sent to Pod IPs or VM IPs?
notes.back: workload (set with istioctl waypoint apply --for workload).
notes.explanation: The other values are service (the default), all (both kinds) and none (no traffic, useful for testing).
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Waypoint traffic types”
notes.evidence: workloadPod IPs or VM IPs allBoth service and workload traffic noneNo traffic (useful for testing) Waypoint selection occurs based on the destination type, service or workload, to which traffic was originally addressed.

notes.front: A deployed waypoint is not used until a namespace, service or pod carries the label {{c1::istio.io/use-waypoint}} with the waypoint’s name as its value.
notes.back: istio.io/use-waypoint
notes.explanation: Most users apply a waypoint to a whole namespace, and the documentation recommends starting that way.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Use a waypoint proxy”
notes.evidence: When a waypoint proxy is deployed, it is not used by any resources until you explicitly configure those resources to use it. To enable a namespace, service or Pod to use a waypoint, add the istio.io/use-waypoint label with a value of the waypoint name.

notes.front: A service is labelled istio.io/use-waypoint=audit, but no waypoint named audit exists. What happens to requests from ambient clients?
notes.back: A: ztunnel routes them directly to the destination, and the waypoint’s Layer 7 policy never takes effect.
notes.choices:
A) ztunnel routes them directly to the destination
B) Requests fail until the waypoint exists
C) istiod creates the waypoint automatically
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: ztunnel routes directly rather than failing the request. C is wrong: istiod only deploys a waypoint once a Gateway resource for it is applied.
notes.explanation: The label records intent but does not guarantee traversal; a policy allowing only the waypoint’s identity makes it mandatory.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Require traffic to traverse the waypoint”
notes.evidence: The istio.io/use-waypoint label records your intent to send traffic through a waypoint, but on its own it does not guarantee that this happens. ztunnel routes traffic directly to the destination, rather than failing the request, when: the named waypoint does not exist or has no address

notes.front: If both a namespace and a service in it carry istio.io/use-waypoint, which waypoint is used?
notes.back: The service’s waypoint, as long as it can handle service or all traffic.
notes.explanation: Likewise, a label on a pod takes precedence over a namespace label.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Use a waypoint proxy”
notes.evidence: If the istio.io/use-waypoint label exists on both a namespace and a service, the service waypoint takes precedence over the namespace waypoint as long as the service waypoint can handle service or all traffic. Similarly, a label on a pod will take precedence over a namespace label.

notes.front: Which extra label lets a resource use a waypoint in a different namespace, and what must that waypoint’s Gateway allow?
notes.back: istio.io/use-waypoint-namespace; the Gateway must allow routes from other namespaces (allowedRoutes.namespaces.from).
notes.explanation: Out of the box a waypoint serves only its own namespace; cross-namespace use is possible from Istio 1.23.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Configure waypoint proxies”, section “Cross-namespace waypoint use”
notes.evidence: It is possible to use a waypoint in another namespace by adding a new label, istio.io/use-waypoint-namespace. istio.io/use-waypoint-namespace works for all resources which support the istio.io/use-waypoint label. Together, the two labels specify the name and namespace of your waypoint respectively.

notes.front: In Istio, how does the job of the data plane differ from that of the control plane?
notes.back: Data plane: proxies that mediate all traffic between services and report telemetry. Control plane: configures those proxies.
notes.explanation: In sidecar mode the control plane is istiod and the data plane is the Envoy sidecars.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Architecture”, introduction
notes.evidence: These proxies mediate and control all network communication between microservices. They also collect and report telemetry on all mesh traffic. The control plane manages and configures the proxies to route traffic.

notes.front: How do ztunnel and a waypoint proxy differ in where they run and what they process?
notes.back: ztunnel: one per node, Layer 4 only. Waypoint: optional Envoy proxy, typically per namespace, adding Layer 7 processing.
notes.explanation: Ambient mode layers them: the ztunnel overlay is always on, and waypoints are added only where Layer 7 features are needed.
notes.source: Istio documentation, “Ambient mode: Overview”, introduction and “How it works”
notes.evidence: Ambient mode splits Istio’s functionality into two distinct layers. At the base, the ztunnel secure overlay handles routing and zero trust security for traffic. Above that, when needed, users can enable L7 waypoint proxies to get access to the full range of Istio features.
